title: Mother of US Green Card Holder Denied Visitor Visa: 214(b) Rules and Interview Tips
excerpt: A Green Card holder's mother was refused a B1/B2 visitor visa within minutes at the Mumbai consulate despite showing savings, property and investments. Reddit users - and the 214(b) rule itself - say it was never about money at all.
body:
• A widowed Indian mother of a US Green Card holder was denied a B1/B2 visa at the Mumbai consulate after a five-minute interview; she cited fixed-deposit savings, property and investments, but the officer asked for no documents and invited her to reapply.
  • The refusal was almost certainly issued under INA Section 214(b), which presumes every applicant intends to immigrate until proven otherwise - officers weigh proof of return (job, property, dependents) far more heavily than proof of funds.
  • Reader utility: file ITRs showing steady income, carry property deeds and an employment letter, keep the itinerary short and specific (2-3 weeks, not a month), and match every DS-160 answer in the interview - then don't reapply until the facts change.
  • Viral Reddit advice says "never say you are funding the trip" - self-funding can read as having nothing anchoring her home - but visa guides say answer funding questions honestly, then pivot to ties: the case is won on roots, not rupees.

A US Green Card holder's mother walked into the Mumbai consulate for a B1/B2 visa interview to attend her daughter's housewarming - and walked out refused, five minutes later. Her account, shared on Reddit and reported by LiveMint, has reignited debate over what consular officers actually look for. The widowed mother, who lives with her son, cited fixed-deposit savings "good enough to cover my one-month trip" and a stay at her daughter's home; the officer asked about purpose, sponsorship, travel history and whether she feared returning to India - then denied the visa without requesting a single document.

214(b): it's about ties, not money

The legal frame is Section 214(b) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, the single most common ground for visitor-visa refusals. It flips the normal burden of proof: every applicant is presumed to be an intending immigrant until they demonstrate otherwise. In practice, officers decide in minutes whether the applicant's life in India is compelling enough to pull them back.

"They care that your mother has the profile of someone they think will return home. To the consular officer, she did not, and it's not hard to see why they made that determination. That's what a 214(b) denial means."

- Reddit user, quoted by LiveMint

The mother's own words illustrate the gap: "I live with my son, so he takes care of my expenses, and I also survive out of the interest from my FD and other investments." To a sympathetic reader, honest. To an officer screening for immigrant intent, commenters argued, it reads as: no job, no steady income, dependent on children - with the wealthier child in America. Asked if she feared returning, she said: "I will return back as I have my son, property here in India, and other community/religious duties." The property was in her name, her daughter wrote - but with no documents requested and no steady income on record, the ties did not register.

What the internet got right - and where it overreached

The thread's sharpest advice - "Never say that you are funding the trip" - is an argument about framing: self-funding, users contended, makes her look like a free agent with nothing to return to, while sponsorship by the daughter keeps the financial story tied to a fixed visit. One user whose mother was approved said they stated clearly that they sponsored the trip, with property in her name.

Visa-prep guides take a more measured line: answer the funding question clearly and honestly - officers ask "who will cover your travel expenses?" as a matter of course - but win the case on ties. The playbook: a clear purpose with dates, documented funds, and undeniable economic, social and family anchors in India. Keep answers short and consistent, matching the DS-160 exactly.

Other suggestions track with professional advice: shorten the stay (a month reads as a move; two to three weeks reads as a visit), file income-tax returns to show a steady financial footprint, and lay out a specific itinerary. The hardest truth: reapplying with the same facts usually produces the same result - only changed circumstances, given time, move the needle.

The diaspora angle

This is a familiar diaspora pain point: Green Card holders who want parents to visit for housewarmings, births and festivals, only to watch the visa refused at the window. There is no appeal from a 214(b) denial - only a fresh application with stronger evidence. Treat the interview as a two-minute pitch with one message: here is my life in India, and here is when I return to it.

What's next

The officer invited the mother to apply again - standard practice, not a promise. The realistic route is materially changed facts: steadier documented income, a shorter and more specific itinerary, and rehearsed answers to the five questions officers always ask - what's your job, why this trip now, who pays, how long, and what brings you back. Short, direct replies beat long explanations; officers test consistency, and confusion reads as risk.

nri_angle: Green Card holders and US citizens inviting parents over must build the case around the parent's roots in India - steady income, property, a short specific itinerary - because a 214(b) denial has no appeal, only a stronger reapplication.
